Such a situation would cause despair and lead many to curse their horrible fate.
But for Zeno of Citium,
it became the foundation of his work and the legacy of his life.
The once-rich merchant lost everything
when he shipwrecked in Athens around 300 BC.
With not much to do, he entered a bookstore,
read about Socrates and became intrigued,
and began to seek out and study with the famous philosophers of the city.
As Zeno started to educate his own students,
he laid the groundwork for the philosophy known as Stoicism,
whose teachings on virtue, tolerance, and self-control
have inspired generations of thinkers and leaders.
The word "Stoicism" comes from the Greek "stoa poikile",
the decorated public colonnade
where Zeno and his disciples gathered for discussions.
Today, we use the word "stoic" colloquially
to refer to someone
who remains calm under pressure and avoids emotional extremes.
But while this reflects important aspects of Stoicism,
the original philosophy was more than just an attitude.
Stoics believed that everything around us
operates according to a web of cause and effect
whose outcome was a rational structure of the universe called logos.
And although we cannot always control the events that affect us,
we can control how we approach things.
Instead of imagining an ideal society,
the stoic tries to deal with the world as it is
while pursuing personal development through four cardinal virtues:
practical wisdom,
the ability to face complex situations
in a logical, grounded, and calm manner;
temperance,
the exercise of self-control and moderation
in all aspects of life;
justice,
treating others fairly even when they have erred,
and courage,
present not only in extraordinary circumstances,
but when facing daily challenges with clarity and integrity.
As Seneca, one of the most famous Roman writers, wrote,
"Sometimes even to live is an act of courage."
But while Stoicism focuses on personal improvement,
it is not an egocentric philosophy.
At a time when Roman laws considered slaves property,
Seneca advocated for humane treatment of them
and emphasized that we all share the same fundamental humanity.
Stoicism also does not promote passivity.
The idea is that only those who cultivated virtue and self-control
can inspire positive change in others.
One of the most famous Stoic writers
was one of the great Roman emperors.
Stoicism helped Marcus Aurelius during his 19-year reign
to lead the Empire while facing two major wars
and to cope with the loss of many of his children.
Centuries later, Marcus's journals would guide and comfort Nelson Mandela
during his 27 years of imprisonment
in his struggle for racial equality in South Africa.
After his release and eventual victory,
Mandela emphasized the importance of peace and reconciliation,
convinced that while the injustices of the past could not be changed,
his people could confront them in the present
to build a better and more just future.
Stoicism was an active school of philosophy
for several centuries in Greece and Rome.
It disappeared as a formal institution,
but it remains an influential philosophy.
Christian theologians, like Thomas Aquinas,
admired and adopted its approach to virtues
and there are similarities between Stoic ataraxia, or tranquility of mind,
and the Buddhist concept of nirvana.
A particularly influential Stoic was the philosopher Epictetus
who wrote that suffering does not arise
from the events of our lives, but from our judgments about them.
This has resonated strongly
in modern psychology and the self-help movement.
For example, rational emotive behavioral therapy
focuses on changing self-destructive attitudes.

There is also Viktor Frankl's logotherapy.
Developed by Frankl himself
based on his experience as a prisoner in a concentration camp,
logotherapy is governed by the Stoic principle
that we can use our willpower
to give meaning to our lives
even in the bleakest situations.
